segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So let us be afraid that, while the promise of entering his rest still remains, any one of you might be found to have fallen short of it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For we too have had good news announced to us, just as they did; but the message they heard did not benefit them, because they were not united by faith with those who listened.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For we who have believed do enter that rest, just as he has said:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “As I swore in my anger, ‘They shall never enter my rest,’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: although his works had been finished since the foundation of the world.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For somewhere he has spoken of the seventh day in this way:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “And God rested on the seventh day from all his works,”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and again in this passage:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “They shall never enter my rest.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Since, then, it remains for some to enter it, and those who formerly had the good news announced to them did not enter because of disobedience,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: he again fixes a certain day—“Today”—saying through David so long afterward, as has been said before,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken afterward about another day.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So then, a Sabbath rest remains for the people of God;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for whoever has entered God’s rest has himself also rested from his works, just as God did from his own.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Let us therefore make every effort to enter that rest, so that no one may fall by following the same example of disobedience.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the word of God is living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing as far as the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and able to judge the thoughts and intentions of the heart.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: No creature is hidden from his sight, but everything is naked and laid bare to the eyes of the one to whom we must give account.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Since, then, we have a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold fast to our confession.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but one who has been tested in every way just as we are, yet without sin.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Let us then approach the throne of grace with confidence, so that we may receive mercy and find grace to help us at the right time.

notes.note: The Greek verb can mean “seem,” “think,” or “be judged.” The rendering takes it in the last sense, of a verdict that someone has missed the promise. Others translate “should seem to have fallen short,” or, less often, “should think he has come too late for it.”

notes.phrase: had good news announced to us
notes.traditional: had the gospel preached to us
notes.note: The verb was an ordinary word for announcing good news, and here it is applied equally to the wilderness generation and to the readers. “Gospel” would suggest a specifically Christian message that Israel in the desert did not hear in that form. Many modern translations already use “good news” here.

notes.phrase: because they were not united by faith with those who listened
notes.traditional: not being mixed with faith in them that heard it
notes.note: The manuscripts differ by one ending. The reading followed here makes the people “not united” with those who listened, probably Joshua and Caleb or believers generally. The other reading makes the message “not combined with faith in those who heard it,” and several major translations follow it. The first has the stronger early manuscript support, though the second gives a smoother sense, and the choice is disputed.

notes.phrase: They shall never enter my rest
notes.note: The Greek literally reads “If they shall enter my rest,” copying a Hebrew oath formula in which the penalty clause is left unspoken. The form amounts to an emphatic denial. The quotation is Psalm 95:11 (94:11 in the Greek Old Testament), which looks back to the wilderness generation barred from Canaan.

In Greek the names Joshua and Jesus are identical (Iēsous). The context, the entry into Canaan, shows that Joshua son of Nun is meant, but a first-century hearer would have caught the echo of Jesus’ name. The older English rendering “Jesus” here is misleading.

The author switches here from the word for “rest” used throughout the passage to a rare noun that occurs nowhere else in the New Testament. In later Greek writers it means Sabbath observance. Some therefore prefer “Sabbath celebration” or “Sabbath keeping,” but “Sabbath rest” is the usual rendering and ties the word to God’s seventh-day rest in verse 4.

The verb is formed from the word for “neck” and occurs only here in the New Testament. Elsewhere it is used of a wrestler seizing an opponent by the neck. The image intended here is uncertain, with suggestions including a wrestler’s hold and a sacrificial victim’s throat bent back and exposed. The general sense of being fully exposed is agreed.

notes.phrase: to whom we must give account
notes.traditional: with whom we have to do
notes.note: The Greek is literally “to whom, for us, the word,” using the same noun, logos, that opens verse 12 (“the word of God”). It can mean “to whom we must render account” or, as a common idiom, “with whom we have to do.” The first fits the judicial imagery of the passage, and either way the author is playing on the two senses of the noun.

The Greek verb means to put to the test, and in the Greek Old Testament it is the standard word for the testing of Israel in the wilderness, the story the author has just been expounding. Modern English “tempt” has narrowed to enticement to sin. Most translations keep “tempted” here, partly because of the following “yet without sin,” and lexicons recognize both senses, so the choice is disputed.

The word originally meant freedom to speak one’s mind and came to mean the assurance of someone who can stand before a superior without fear or shame. “Boldness” can suggest nerve or audacity, which is not the point. Several modern versions also have “confidence” here, and the difference is one of English nuance, not a dispute about meaning.

candidates.reason: Older versions render it “unbelief” and it sits close to ἀπιστία in Hebrews 3–4 and Romans 11, so the disobedience/unbelief line needs fixing across books.
It recurs in Hebrews, 2 Corinthians and 1 Timothy, and translators vary between “confession,” “profession” and “the faith we profess,” while “confession” may suggest admitting sins to modern readers.
It is a pervasive term whose rendering (“grace,” “favor,” “gift,” “thanks”) varies by sense and needs one policy for the whole New Testament.
It appears in this chapter in three senses (message, word of God, account), and its handling affects wordplay and consistency across the New Testament.
It alternates between “weakness,” “illness” and “infirmity” across the Gospels and the letters, and readers would benefit from a fixed rule on where each applies.
